title: Chicago's Rum Boogie in 1945: Otis, Norris Turney and Luther Henderson
summary: They open at the Rum Boogie with Norris Turney and Otis White, whose tone pierces the brass, and Luther Henderson writes arrangements.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: But when they just had that lower budget, see, they were able to sustain -- you know what I mean -- a little loss here, and a little loss there, you know what I mean, see, and just keep going. That's what's happened. And we stayed at the Club Riviera all through that year, and we drew people, see. And things got a little dead just before Christmas. Our contract ran out on the tenth of January. The following weekend, we opened at the Rum Boogie in Chicago. This was in 1945. We opened at the Rum Boogie, and the band went over real great. We had a great band. The band had worked back up, and we had -- we hired Norris Turney, who played with Duke. He played flute, clarinet, alto sax, and we had Otis -- this alto player. I'll tell you what he could do, Otis, with the saxophone. You could have the whole eight brass playing as loud as they want to back there, Otis could blow and his tone could pierce the brass section.

That's how great a tone he had. He could sing through anything. The man just had -- he was just a great alto saxophone player. Now, he was no virtuoso, also, see, but he had that tone. And you had -- he was a slow reader, and that -- he always was that. He never did improve too much on this. But once he got something, he had it, man, he could lead that section. My brother Charles would tell you the same thing. He was something to hear.
We opened in Chicago's Rum Boogie. My brother Charles
had told me about Luther Henderson being a great writer. And we had Luther to write our arrangements for us on 'Lady Be Good.' You remember 'Lady Be Good?'

And we rehearsed that thing, and we rehearsed that thing, and I told Otis, 'Otis, you take it home with you. I said, 'You go to bed with it, get up with it. You can play it, I know you can play it.' Otis got so he could play that song. We changed pianos. We had a boy named John Carter on the piano. In that band, we had John Carter on the piano, we had Bill Martin on trumpet, on the bass -- who did we have on bass?
I know you had some Spanish boy playing trombone, married Hortense's sister.

We had Fernando. We got him from Noble Sissel. And we did have Big Chief, the trombone player that now plays with Lester Lanin, the society bandleader? That plays all over America? Well, Big Chief, their trombone player, [Russell Moore]-ed. Indian, used to play with us. We did have him, but he left us. And we had -- I'm trying to think who we had on trumpet. We picked up a boy in Chicago. Beautiful trumpet player. He used to play with Jimmy Lunsford. They later found that he was -- you know, and so we had to let him go. But when he felt good,

man, he was great.

And we had another little boy in Chicago, used to sing.
